title: Ratio, Root, and Alternating Series Tests

questions.q: Use the Ratio Test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n}{2^n}$ converges.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{(n+1)/2^{n+1}}{n/2^n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n+1}{2n}=\frac{1}{2}<1$. Converges by the Ratio Test.

questions.q: Use the Ratio Test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n!}{3^n}$ converges.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{(n+1)!/3^{n+1}}{n!/3^n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n+1}{3}=\infty>1$. Diverges by the Ratio Test.

questions.q: Use the Root Test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{n}{2n+1}\right)^n$ converges.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\sqrt[n]{\left|\left(\frac{n}{2n+1}\right)^n\right|}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n}{2n+1}=\frac{1}{2}<1$. Converges by the Root Test.

sections.heading: Alternating series and the Alternating Series Test

questions.q: State the Alternating Series Test, and use it to show $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ converges.
questions.answer: The AST states $\sum(-1)^{n+1}b_n$ converges if $b_n>0$, $b_n$ is decreasing, and $\lim_{n\to\infty}b_n=0$. Here $b_n=\frac{1}{n}$: positive, decreasing, and $\to0$. The series converges (this is the alternating harmonic series).

questions.q: Determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n n}{n+1}$ converges using the Alternating Series Test.
questions.answer: $b_n=\frac{n}{n+1}\to1\neq0$. Since $b_n$ does not approach $0$, the Alternating Series Test does not apply, and in fact the series diverges by the $n$th-term test.

questions.q: Approximate $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$ using the first 4 terms, and bound the error using the Alternating Series Error Bound.
Determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$ converges absolutely, conditionally, or diverges.
questions.answer: $\sum\left|\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}\right|=\sum\frac{1}{n^2}$, a convergent p-series ($p=2>1$). So the series converges ABSOLUTELY.

questions.q: Determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ converges absolutely, conditionally, or diverges.
questions.answer: $\sum\left|\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\right|=\sum\frac{1}{n}$, the harmonic series, which diverges. But the alternating series itself converges (shown earlier by the AST). So it converges CONDITIONALLY.

questions.q: Use the Ratio Test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{3^n}{n!}$ converges.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{3^{n+1}/(n+1)!}{3^n/n!}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{3}{n+1}=0<1$. Converges by the Ratio Test.

questions.q: Explain why the Ratio Test is INCONCLUSIVE for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}$, and identify which test should be used instead.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n}{n+1}=1$. Since the limit equals exactly $1$, the Ratio Test gives no conclusion. The p-series test (or Integral Test) should be used instead, correctly showing divergence.

sections.heading: Partial sums of an alternating series (visualizing oscillating convergence)

questions.q: Compute the first 5 partial sums of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ (the alternating harmonic series, which converges to $\ln2\approx0.693$), and describe how they oscillate.
questions.answer: $S_1=1$, $S_2=1-\frac{1}{2}=0.5$, $S_3=0.5+\frac{1}{3}\approx0.833$, $S_4\approx0.833-0.25=0.583$, $S_5\approx0.583+0.2=0.783$. The partial sums oscillate above and below the true sum $\ln2\approx0.693$, with each successive sum landing closer — a signature behavior of alternating series.

sections.heading: Determining the number of terms needed for a given accuracy

questions.q: For $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^3}$, find the minimum number of terms needed so the partial sum is within $0.001$ of the true sum, using the Alternating Series Error Bound.
questions.answer: Need $b_{n+1}=\frac{1}{(n+1)^3}<0.001 \Rightarrow (n+1)^3>1000 \Rightarrow n+1>10 \Rightarrow n\geq10$. So $10$ terms suffice.

questions.q: Classify each series as convergent (state absolutely or conditionally) or divergent:
answers: Conditionally convergent — converges by AST ($b_n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\to0$, decreasing), but $\sum\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ diverges ($p=\frac{1}{2}\leq1$)
Conditionally convergent — converges by AST, but $\sum\frac{n^2}{n^3+1}$ diverges by Limit Comparison to $\sum\frac{1}{n}$
Absolutely convergent — $\sum\frac{1}{n!}$ converges by the Ratio Test (ratio $\to0$)

sections.heading: The Root Test with more complex expressions

questions.q: Use the Root Test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2n+1}{3n-1}\right)^n$ converges.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\sqrt[n]{\left(\frac{2n+1}{3n-1}\right)^n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2n+1}{3n-1}=\frac{2}{3}<1$. Converges by the Root Test.

questions.q: Use the Root Test to determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2^n}{n^n}$ converges.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\sqrt[n]{\frac{2^n}{n^n}}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2}{n}=0<1$. Converges by the Root Test.

sections.heading: Why the Ratio Test fails for p-series

questions.q: Show that the Ratio Test is inconclusive for EVERY p-series $\sum\frac{1}{n^p}$, regardless of $p$.
questions.answer: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{1/(n+1)^p}{1/n^p}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^p=1^p=1$ for ANY value of $p$. Since the limit always equals exactly $1$, the Ratio Test can never determine convergence or divergence for p-series — a different test (the p-series test itself) is required.

sections.heading: Combining multiple tests in one problem

questions.q: Determine whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-2)^n}{n^2}$ converges absolutely, conditionally, or diverges.
questions.answer: Test absolute convergence with the Ratio Test on $\left|\frac{(-2)^n}{n^2}\right|=\frac{2^n}{n^2}$: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{2^{n+1}/(n+1)^2}{2^n/n^2}\right|=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2n^2}{(n+1)^2}=2>1$. Diverges (even in absolute value) — so the original series DIVERGES (the terms don't even approach $0$ since $|a_n|\to\infty$).
